rv.q: This new ‘Spamalot’ arrives, beefed up, gussied up and yes, even funnier than in its birthing engagement earlier this year...the revival of the Tony-winning musical by Python great Eric Idle, with John Du Prez, brings joy to a land desperately short of guffaws and chuckles and snickers and giggles.
The production is so richly stocked with prime talent that there isn’t a smidgen of a lull in the proceedings.
This one, directed and choreographed by Josh Rhodes, gives the “ni”-sayers what they want.
The revival has lost none of the smart-dumb charm of either the original musical or its great source of inspiration – the beloved 1975 film Monty Python and the Holy Grail.
Not so with Spamalot, a show that works both as a vessel for Monty Python nostalgia and a platform for the comic talents of this generation of Broadway performers.
There is something liberating for both artists and audiences about a Broadway show that refuses, even for a moment, to take itself seriously.

This is the showcase role that longtime Kritzer fans—another group that includes, full disclosure, me—have been waiting for, and she grabs it by the throat in a full-tilt comedic and vocal tour de force, culminating in the delightfully ostentatious "Diva's Lament."

In the Broadway landscape of 2023, Spamalot turns out to be oddly well positioned to lure people in with the promise of the quotably familiar, then blast them in the face with a confetti cannon full of THEATER (and literal confetti).

Idle’s comic genius remains entirely evident here and he and Du Prez came up with the kind of brassy, swirling score that screamed Big Night Out on Broadway, even as it lampooned everything from scantily clad choruses to divas devolving in Act 2.
Never hilarious, the revival stalls out at pleasant.
But that grail is not to be found here.
The only problem with Spamalot is that it has to end.
The real star of the show is the divine Leslie Rodriguez Kritzer as the Lady of the Lake in what deserves to be a Tony Award-winning turn.
...the new iteration of the Monty Python funfest is a welcome dose of both hilarious deconstruction and old-fashioned razzle-dazzle.
Monty Python is timeless, and this Spamalot revival just proves the staying power of its humor.
It rarely gets any better than this.
Spamalot has no quarter for sadness; it's a fortress of merrymaking that won't let anything serious breach its walls.
Spamalot—the 2005. Tony-winning Best Musical “lovingly ripped off” (as the tagline sayeth) from the 1975 low-budget British movie—is back on Broadway, and it’s as wonderfully silly as ever.
If this production, under the direction of Josh Rhodes, has a fault, it’s that the staging can sometimes be too tongue in cheek for its own good.

Spamalot’s expertly written and performed silliness is endless, beguiling, and winning, and so well-done that—despite the gay and Jewish clunkers of songs—the musical remains a daffy, rollicking night out.
“Spamalot” is high-stepping, low-brow and often hilarious.

Even peppered with choreographic references to an iconic Drag Race lip sync and the sounds of Grindr notifications, Lancelot’s big coming-out disco number is more or less a relic, amusing primarily through the gauze of nostalgia.

But alas, as with many other whose near-two-decade cobwebs were only lightly dusted off, I was left to consume a number about a character’s coming out that, until the final moments when a few Grindr beeps came through, comprised what a 2005 straight man’s idea of gayness was like.
The mustiness now is downright allergy-inducing.
Brilliantly directed by Rhodes, 'Spamalot' is diverting and entertaining.
A Medieval comedic throwdown you won't want to miss.
A safe "Spamalot" doesn't lack shelf-life in 2023, but it could be funnier.
Delightful for some, confusing for others.

cn.t: Critics mostly embrace this energetic revival as hilarious escapism with a stellar comic cast, though some find the nearly 50-year-old Python humor feels dated and the production adds little new to the 2005 original.

sg.ra: Rows B-L are the house's actual sweet-spot band — Row A loses legroom and cranes necks because the St. James stage is raised on multiple recent productions (Sunset's LED wall, Something Rotten!'s set), while Row L is the last row before both the shallow rake AND the mezzanine overhang bite into the view Rows M+ hit the St. James's signature rake-and-overhang double-whammy — shorter patrons report 'craning around heads' and top-of-stage cutoff; a below-average experience for a 1,710-seat house

The Row D aisle-angled seats (D1/D2) are a genuine St. James unicorn — the row is set at a different angle than the rows in front so no seat sits directly ahead of you; this bypasses the flat-rake problem that defines the rest of the house 'Partial view' labeled seats in rows A-C side orchestra are heavily production-dependent — Into The Woods and Sunset (downstage-centric) work fine; Frozen's left-side set wall and Something Rotten!'s spread staging defeat them Back rows Q-S side orchestra sit directly under the mezzanine overhang — OK view of downstage action but top-of-set elements (screens, signage) cut off

Front mezzanine (Row A) is frequently called the best seat in the 1,710-seat house — Wikipedia notes the mezz 'extends over what were originally the tenth row of orchestra seats,' so you're unusually close for an upper tier, and because the orchestra's rake is so shallow, veterans repeatedly prefer Row A mezz to mid-orchestra at this specific house Row A has two specific St. James quirks that are production-sensitive — a low brass railing and an extension lighting rig on the mezz front; fine for average height but shorter patrons hit them, and Sunset Boulevard's onstage-lip blocking can make Row A worse than Row B-C

Front rows A-C side mezzanine are the house's best discount — St. James veterans (Patash: 'Gypsy, Bullets Over Broadway, A Funny Thing Happened... my favorite seats... I don't mind the side section in the least') buy them deliberately over pricier orchestra for every major musical High-seat-number side mezz (>18 in rows B-F) hits the mezzanine curvature problem — not just off-angle but the row pitches away from the stage creating sub-inch knee clearance Row B seat 18 area (where pricing typically breaks to a cheaper bracket) is a genuine value sweet spot — view is nearly identical to Row A but noticeably cheaper; confirmed across multiple productions

Rear mezz is the house's classic value trap — priced as mezzanine but the rake flattens and you're a third of the way back in a 1,710-seat house; reviewers describe needing seat boosters and sliding to the seat edge to see anything. Row Q aisle has an additional specific quirk: a corridor-exit light stays on during the show. Row J is the one exception in the rear-mezz block — it's the first row of a rear bank with a walkway in front, so no heads block the view; veterans specifically target it as the discount version of front mezz

Row A center balcony is the upper-tier's saving grace — BWW veterans split sharply (one calls it 'one of the worst balconies on Broadway', others swear by it), but the consensus lands on Row A specifically because the no-lean position, sound improvement from the extra speaker truss, and low railing make it better than rear mezz for the same price The balcony is a physical climb — 'like climbing a tower' — and is the second balcony; older patrons or anyone with mobility should not attempt at this house specifically Row A is the ONLY row that reliably clears the railing — behind Row A the rail bisects the stage; chain-reaction lean-forward effect forces everyone below to follow suit

Side balcony behind Row A combines every St. James hazard in one seat — side-angle, railing blocking downstage, second-balcony height, tight legroom, and (per multiple patrons) lottery-only sales because the house knows they're problematic Row A side balcony aisle seats (1-3 L, 2-4 R) are the one exception — sightlines avoid the railing, you're 'almost right over the front of the mezzanine,' and legroom is usable; anything behind Row A or away from the aisle is genuinely skip-tier at this house because back side-balcony also carries sound-mix issues off-axis from the speaker truss

vr.q: I don't know if it's worth top Broadway ticket prices, but it's certainly a fun night out, especially if you never got to see the original production!
Overall, this is still not a show for me. Um, but I did feel like a lot of the character choices and a lot of the improv made it worth going to see again and made it like that much more enjoyable.
I don't find the material itself to be worth your average Broadway ticket price. the laughs were cheap, and the music sounded cheap.
